html:
SMTO-FIL-0030 — A folder in the copy's path is a link, not a real folder

GUID: 7d7d43f5-c921-4b22-9440-b1fc064acd4c
Slug: file-unsafe-transfer-path
Domain: FIL · Subsystem: files

What happened

  • SMTO stopped the copy because a folder on the way to the file is a link or junction pointing elsewhere on the Windows computer. SMTO only copies through ordinary folders, so files can't land somewhere unexpected.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. On the Windows computer, open the folders in the path from Technical details and look for one shown with a small shortcut arrow on its icon. A folder with that arrow is a link or junction, and SMTO won't copy through it.
  2. Ask SMTO to copy again using the real folder that the link points to, or choose a different destination folder. A path made only of ordinary folders passes this safety check.
  3. If you can't find the linked folder, open Technical details in this panel and select Copy error details. The details list the exact paths SMTO was trying to use.

What success looks like

  • The copy finishes and the file appears in the destination folder.

If it still fails

  • Send the copied error details to the person who manages that Gateway computer. If this copy is part of a saved Run, change its folder yourself or with whoever set it up; don't let it quietly point at a different folder or Gateway.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • On a Windows Gateway, transfer parent pinning found a path component whose type is not an ordinary directory (a symlink, junction or other reparse point), so the transfer refused to traverse it.

What this means

  • Windows transfer parent pinning found a parent whose actual type is not an ordinary directory, refusing unsafe link/reparse traversal. File and transfer receipts retain per-item execution, publication, cleanup and partial-effect facts. These explanations do not modify files, weaken path guards or replay a write; reconcile the original state before further mutation.

Why this can happen

  • Windows transfer parent pinning found a parent whose actual type is not an ordinary directory, refusing unsafe link/reparse traversal.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect each current parent type and the exact intended destination without following rejected reparse points.

How to fix it

  • On the Windows Gateway, inspect each parent of the source and destination path with dir /AL or fsutil reparsepoint query, and use a path whose parents are all ordinary directories (for example the junction's real target). The reparse-point check in transfer_paths.pinned_parent has no override; keep the transfer path guards enabled.
  • Choose source and destination paths inside the authorized transfer boundaries.

Retry and execution caution

  • Apply the correction and confirm the relevant state before requesting another attempt. Prior completed work remains governed by its receipts.

How to verify the fix

  • The transfer uses pinned ordinary parents within its authorized boundaries.

What not to do

  • Do not silently substitute a different target for a saved run or move its existing execution authority.

Technical notes

  • File and transfer receipts retain per-item execution, publication, cleanup and partial-effect facts. These explanations do not modify files, weaken path guards or replay a write; reconcile the original state before further mutation.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
